convictions.notes: CORRECTION TO A COMMON ERROR: the 49 convictions are not a single 2003 event. 48 counts were entered in November 2003 and sentenced that December; the 49th followed in February 2011 after Marrero's remains were located in December 2010. Accounts that report '49 consecutive life sentences in December 2003' merge two proceedings seven years apart.

attributed_victim_count.notes: The Green River Task Force worked a larger set of open cases than the 49 charged, but no agency-published attribution figure with a stated methodology has been retrieved. A contributor should cite a specific King County Sheriff's Office or task force document, or leave this null.

claimed_victim_count.notes: Ridgway gave varying figures during the interviews conducted under the plea agreement, and higher numbers (71, 80 and above) circulate in secondary accounts. No single authoritative transcript citation has been retrieved, and his self-report is in any case unreliable — see adjudication.confession_reliability. Left null rather than importing a number from press synthesis.

estimate_provenance.value: Figures above 49 originate in Ridgway's own statements during plea-agreement interviews and in press synthesis of task force caseload, not in a published agency accounting.

first_known_offence.notes: The first recoveries from the Green River occurred in July and August 1982 and gave the case its name. Exact ordering of the earliest offences rests on later reconstruction.

last_known_offence.notes: Charged offences cluster in the 1980s, with disputed later cases. No reliable terminal date established; a contributor should work from the charging documents rather than secondary chronologies.

jurisdictions.notes: Reichert led the Green River Task Force and later became King County Sheriff. A participant account: valuable for what he witnessed, unreliable on his own significance.

family_structure.notes: Accounts of a dominating mother and a humiliating childhood are ubiquitous in secondary literature but trace to Ridgway's own post-arrest statements and to defence mitigation material. No contemporaneous record retrieved. This is the field where retrospective offender self-report is least reliable and most eagerly repeated.

education.value: Completed secondary education in the Seattle area; repeated years owing to documented learning difficulties.

The employer is the Kenworth truck works; the municipality is not settled here and the value is left at the level the sources agree on. Analytically the relevant fact is the stability: three decades of uninterrupted shift work across the entire offending period.

enuresis.notes: Widely asserted in secondary literature and treated there as formative. It traces to post-arrest self-report and defence mitigation, not to a medical or contemporaneous record. Left null. NOTE: the triad is not a predictor of violence — see the field description in the schema.

animal_cruelty.notes: No documentation located. The frequently repeated account of a stabbing committed in adolescence is a separate matter from animal cruelty and is not recorded here without a citable source.

formal_diagnoses.notes: Ridgway pleaded guilty; there was no trial at which competing psychiatric evidence was tested, and no court-adopted diagnosis has been retrieved. Defence experts produced mitigation assessments that were never adjudicated. Labels applied in secondary literature appear under commentary_attributions.

competency_findings.notes: Competency was not a contested issue in the reported proceedings; no finding retrieved.

psychometric_results.notes: An IQ of 82 is asserted almost universally in secondary accounts. No instrument, administering clinician or date has been located for it. Under this schema a bare IQ number is inadmissible. This figure is load-bearing in popular narratives — it underwrites the 'low-intelligence killer who nonetheless evaded capture' framing — which is precisely why it should not be recorded without provenance.

commentary_attributions.notes: Claims about the discourse surrounding the subject, not about the subject. Not diagnostic data.

victim_selection.value: Offences targeted women working in street prostitution and young women in unstable housing along a highway corridor south of Seattle. The operative feature is institutional: this was a population whose disappearances were reported late, investigated slowly, and in some cases not recorded as suspicious at all.

sources.citation: Guillen, Tomas. Serial Killers: Issues Explored Through the Green River Murders. Pearson Prentice Hall, 2007.

victim_selection.notes: Recorded as an access condition the offender exploited, not as a characteristic of the victims that explains their deaths. Guillen, who covered the case as a reporter, is explicit that the investigative response was shaped by who the victims were. See investigation.detection_delay_factors.

approach_method.notes: Detailed approach accounts derive from Ridgway's plea-agreement interviews. Given the reliability problems recorded under confession_reliability, these are not entered as established behaviour without corroboration from charging documents.

sources.citation: Canter, David and Paul Larkin. 'The Environmental Range of Serial Rapists.' Journal of Environmental Psychology 13(1), 1993, 63-69.

spatial_pattern.notes: Coded as marauder: offences, residence and workplace fall within a compact corridor in south King County, in contrast to USA-001-BUNDY. The coding is the maintainer's application of the Canter & Larkin framework, not a source-attested fact. Note the analytic point — the offender with the narrow geographic range evaded detection far longer than the multi-state one, which cuts against the assumption that mobility drives evasion.

sources.citation: Reichert, David. Chasing the Devil: My Twenty-Year Quest to Capture the Green River Killer. Little, Brown, 2004.

signature_behaviour.notes: Accounts of recurring non-functional conduct derive from the interviews conducted under the 2003 plea agreement. Those interviews were given under an agreement that spared his life, and the corroboration requirement applied to charged offences, not to descriptive detail. No independently documented recurring element has been retrieved. Left null.

post_offence_behaviour.notes: Accounts of returning to deposition sites derive from Ridgway's own statements. Not independently corroborated. Graphic detail is in any case excluded under ETHICS.md.

forensic_countermeasures.value: Use of multiple dispersed deposition sites; introduction of unrelated material at scenes.

sources.citation: Reichert, David. Chasing the Devil: My Twenty-Year Quest to Capture the Green River Killer. Little, Brown, 2004.

forensic_countermeasures.notes: Recorded at the level the source supports. Popular accounts attribute an elaborate deliberate counter-forensic strategy to him; that framing is not adopted here.

motive_classification.notes: Maintainer coding, not a source-attested fact. The framework is cited as the instrument applied, not as authority for this subject's motive. Canter et al. (2004) is cited as the standing methodological caution on typologies of this family. Contributors coding this case differently should record the disagreement rather than overwrite: divergent coding of the same record is a finding. This coding is weaker than the Bundy one and should be treated sceptically: it rests substantially on Ridgway's own account of his motives, which is the class of evidence this dataset treats as least reliable. A contributor may reasonably code this 'hedonistic (lust)' instead.

detection_delay_factors.value: Ridgway was identified as a suspect, interviewed, and sampled early in the investigation, and was nonetheless released for over a decade. The delay was not caused by geographic mobility — his range was compact — but by the limits of contemporaneous forensic technology, by a task force overwhelmed with unindexed paper records, and by an investigative response shaped by the low institutional priority given to the victims.

sources.citation: Egger, Steven A. 'A Working Definition of Serial Murder and the Reduction of Linkage Blindness.' Journal of Police Science and Administration 12(3), 1984, 348-357.
Guillen, Tomas. Serial Killers: Issues Explored Through the Green River Murders. Pearson Prentice Hall, 2007.

detection_delay_factors.notes: This case is the counter-example to linkage blindness as the standard explanation. The linkage was made — the killings were recognised as one series almost immediately, and the correct suspect was in the file. What failed was the ability to convert suspicion into proof, and the willingness to prioritise the cases.

identifying_evidence.value: A saliva sample taken from Ridgway in 1987 was matched, after advances in DNA typing, to biological evidence from three of the earliest victims.

sources.citation: NBC News / Associated Press. 'Washington man admits 48 murders.' 5 November 2003.
Reichert, David. Chasing the Devil: My Twenty-Year Quest to Capture the Green River Killer. Little, Brown, 2004.

identifying_evidence.notes: The decisive material was collected fourteen years before it could be used. The specific typing method should be cited from the laboratory report by a contributor who retrieves it; the widely repeated 'STR' attribution is not confirmed here.

forensic_methods_used.value: DNA typing of retained 1987 reference material. A polygraph examination was administered during the 1980s investigation and Ridgway was reported to have passed it.

sources.citation: Reichert, David. Chasing the Devil: My Twenty-Year Quest to Capture the Green River Killer. Little, Brown, 2004.

method_now_disputed.value: Polygraphy has no established validity as a lie-detection instrument. The 2003 National Research Council review found the scientific evidence insufficient to support its use for security screening or as a determinant of truthfulness. A passed polygraph contributed to Ridgway's elimination as a priority suspect during the 1980s.

sources.citation: National Research Council. The Polygraph and Lie Detection. Washington DC: National Academies Press, 2003.
Reichert, David. Chasing the Devil: My Twenty-Year Quest to Capture the Green River Killer. Little, Brown, 2004.

method_now_disputed.notes: Popular accounts treat the passed polygraph as evidence of Ridgway's composure or 'low cognitive stress'. That reading assumes the instrument works. It does not. The correct inference is about the instrument, not the subject — and this case is among the strongest available demonstrations of it.

arrest.value: Arrested 30 November 2001 in King County, Washington.

sources.citation: NBC News / Associated Press. 'Washington man admits 48 murders.' 5 November 2003.

interrogation_method.value: Following the DNA identification, a plea agreement negotiated by King County Prosecutor Norm Maleng and signed on 13 June 2003 required Ridgway to disclose additional offences, with admissions to be corroborated by physical evidence, in exchange for the State not seeking the death penalty. Extended interviews were conducted under that agreement.

interrogation_method.notes: The corroboration requirement is the analytically important term: unlike the Lucas confessions (see docs/investigative-failures.md), admissions here could not close a case on Ridgway's word alone. The 2011 conviction shows the mechanism working — he had admitted the Marrero killing in 2003, and the conviction followed only when her remains were located in December 2010.

confession_reliability.value: Low as to counts and detail; constrained as to charged offences. Statements were made under an agreement that spared his life, giving a direct incentive to maximise disclosure. The corroboration requirement limited the damage: charged counts rest on physical evidence, not on his account alone.
